title: Lamb Curry
description: A warming British curry-house style lamb curry simmered until tender in a spiced tomato and yogurt sauce.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
ingredients: 650 g lamb shoulder, cut into 3 cm pieces
instructions: Season the lamb with salt, then brown it in hot oil in a heavy pan so the outside takes on colour before the long simmer begins.
Add the sliced onions to the same pan and cook slowly until golden, scraping the browned lamb bits from the base for deeper curry flavour.
Stir in garlic and ginger for one minute, then add curry powder, cumin, coriander, and chilli so the spices bloom in the oil.
Return the lamb to the pan with chopped tomatoes and stock, stirring until the meat is coated in a thick red curry base.
Cover and simmer gently until the lamb is nearly tender, checking occasionally so the sauce reduces slowly rather than catching.
Whisk the yogurt until smooth, then stir it in over low heat to enrich the sauce without splitting the curry.
Simmer uncovered until the lamb is fully tender and the sauce clings to the pieces, adjusting salt and chilli to taste.
Rest the curry for ten minutes, scatter with coriander, and serve with steamed rice or naan while the sauce is glossy.

title: Sausage Casserole
description: A homely British sausage casserole with browned sausages, beans, vegetables, and a rich tomato gravy.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
ingredients: Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: Brown the sausages in a wide casserole until deeply coloured on all sides, then lift them out so they stay juicy later.
Cook the onion, carrots, and celery in the same pan until softened, using the sausage fat to build a savoury base.
Add the garlic and tomato paste, stirring for a minute so the paste darkens slightly and loses its raw edge.
Pour in chopped tomatoes and stock, then add Worcestershire sauce, thyme, bay leaf, and a good pinch of seasoning.
Return the sausages to the casserole, nestling them into the sauce so they finish cooking gently and evenly.
Simmer uncovered until the sauce thickens and the sausages are cooked through, stirring occasionally around the edges.
Fold in the drained beans for the final ten minutes so they warm through without breaking apart in the sauce.
Remove the bay leaf, taste the gravy, and serve the casserole hot with mashed potatoes or crusty bread.

title: Bubble and Squeak
description: A crisp-edged British leftover potato and cabbage cake cooked in butter until golden and savoury.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
ingredients: 250 g cooked cabbage or Brussels sprouts, chopped
instructions: Warm the butter and oil in a heavy frying pan, then cook the onion until soft and lightly golden around the edges.
Mix the mashed potato with chopped cabbage, salt, pepper, and parsley until the greens are evenly spread through the potato.
Spoon the potato mixture into the pan and press it into a thick even cake so maximum surface touches the hot base.
Cook without moving it for several minutes until the underside forms a deep golden crust and releases from the pan.
Turn the mixture in rough sections, pressing it back down so more potato makes contact and creates extra crisp bits.
Continue cooking and turning until the centre is piping hot and the outside has several browned, crunchy patches.
Taste a small spoonful and adjust seasoning carefully, remembering leftover potatoes may already contain butter and salt.
Serve immediately with eggs, bacon, or roasted tomatoes while the edges are crisp and the centre remains soft.

title: Welsh Rarebit
description: A classic Welsh cheese toast with mustard, ale, and Worcestershire sauce grilled until bubbling.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
instructions: Toast the bread lightly on both sides first so it can support the rich topping without turning soggy underneath.
Melt the butter in a small pan, stir in the flour, and cook for a minute to make a smooth base for the cheese sauce.
Whisk in the ale gradually until the mixture thickens, then reduce the heat before adding cheese so it melts gently.
Stir in mustard, Worcestershire sauce, cayenne, and black pepper until the rarebit mixture is glossy and savoury.
Take the pan off the heat and beat in the egg yolk quickly, which helps the topping set under the grill.
Spread the cheese mixture thickly over each toast slice, reaching right to the edges so the bread does not burn.
Grill until the topping bubbles, browns in spots, and smells deeply toasted while the centre stays creamy.
Rest for one minute before serving, because the cheese will be extremely hot and thick straight from the grill.

title: Scotch Eggs
description: Jammy boiled eggs wrapped in seasoned sausage meat, crumbed, and fried until crisp and golden.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
instructions: Boil the eggs until just set with a slightly soft centre, then chill them quickly in cold water before peeling carefully.
Mix the sausage meat with parsley, mustard, salt, and pepper until evenly seasoned but still loose and tender.
Divide the sausage mixture into six portions and flatten each one into a thin oval on a piece of cling film.
Wrap each peeled egg in sausage meat, sealing the joins fully so no egg is exposed during frying.
Roll the wrapped eggs first in flour, then beaten egg, and finally breadcrumbs for a crisp even coating.
Heat oil to a steady medium temperature so the coating browns while the sausage cooks through around the egg.
Fry the Scotch eggs in batches, turning gently until golden all over and cooked through to the centre.
Drain on kitchen paper, season lightly, and serve warm or cool with mustard, salad, or pickles.

title: Full English Breakfast
description: A classic fry-up plate with sausages, bacon, eggs, beans, tomatoes, mushrooms, and toast.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
ingredients: Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: Start the sausages in a large pan over medium heat, turning regularly so they brown evenly and cook through without splitting.
Add the bacon beside the sausages and fry until the fat renders and the edges become crisp but the meat stays tender.
Warm the baked beans gently in a small saucepan, stirring now and then so the sauce does not catch on the bottom.
Cook the tomatoes cut side down and the mushrooms in a little butter until softened, browned, and seasoned well.
Toast or fry the bread according to preference, keeping it warm while the rest of the breakfast finishes.
Fry the eggs in oil and butter until the whites are set and the yolks remain soft, seasoning only at the end.
Check the sausages are fully cooked, then arrange all components on warm plates in generous separate sections.
Serve immediately with extra toast and tea, because a full English breakfast is best while every part is still hot.

title: Kedgeree
description: A gently spiced British breakfast rice dish with smoked haddock, curry powder, peas, and boiled eggs.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
ingredients: Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: Poach the smoked haddock gently in milk until it flakes easily, then lift it out and reserve a little poaching milk.
Melt butter in a wide pan and cook the onion until soft, sweet, and lightly golden without letting it burn.
Stir in curry powder for a minute so the spices warm through and coat the onions evenly in the butter.
Add the cooked rice and a splash of reserved poaching milk, folding carefully so the grains stay separate.
Flake the haddock into large pieces and fold it through the rice with the peas until everything is hot.
Season with lemon juice, salt, and pepper, tasting carefully because smoked haddock can already be salty.
Nestle the boiled egg quarters on top and warm them briefly with the lid on rather than breaking them into the rice.
Finish with parsley and serve at once, keeping the fish flakes visible and the rice light rather than wet.

title: Fish and Chips
description: Crisp battered white fish served with thick chips, peas, and lemon in true chip-shop style.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
ingredients: 4 cod or haddock fillets, about 160 g each
900 g potatoes, cut into thick chips
250 ml cold beer or sparkling water
Lemon wedges and peas, to serve
instructions: Rinse the cut potatoes, dry them thoroughly, and blanch them in medium-hot oil until tender but still pale.
Whisk flour, cornstarch, baking powder, salt, and pepper, then add cold beer to make a light batter just before frying.
Pat the fish fillets completely dry and dust them lightly with flour so the batter grips the surface evenly.
Raise the oil temperature and fry the chips a second time until crisp, golden, and fluffy in the centre.
Dip each fish fillet into the batter, let excess drip off, and lower it carefully into the hot oil.
Fry the fish until the batter is puffed, deeply golden, and the fish flakes easily when tested at the thickest point.
Drain fish and chips on a rack, not paper only, so steam does not soften the crisp coating.
Season immediately with salt and serve with peas, lemon wedges, and malt vinegar while the batter crackles.

title: Coronation Chicken
description: Cold poached chicken folded through a curried mayonnaise with mango chutney, raisins, and almonds.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
ingredients: Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: Poach or roast the chicken until just cooked through, then cool it completely before shredding into generous bite-size pieces.
Stir mayonnaise, yogurt, mango chutney, curry powder, and lemon juice together until smooth and lightly golden.
Taste the dressing before adding chicken, adjusting salt, pepper, curry powder, or lemon so it is balanced.
Fold the shredded chicken through the dressing gently so every piece is coated without becoming mashed.
Add raisins, almonds, and spring onions, keeping a few almonds back for a crisp garnish at the end.
Chill the mixture for at least twenty minutes so the curry flavour softens and the chicken absorbs the dressing.
Stir once more before serving and loosen with a spoonful of yogurt if the salad has thickened too much.
Serve with salad leaves, jacket potatoes, sandwiches, or a rice salad, finishing with the reserved almonds.

title: Ploughman's Lunch
description: A classic British no-cook lunch board with cheese, bread, pickle, apple, salad, and chutney.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
instructions: Choose a large board or plate and place the cheddar as the central ingredient, leaving room for bread and pickles.
Slice the bread thickly and butter it lightly, keeping the pieces rustic rather than arranging them too formally.
Add the pickle and chutney in small bowls or neat spoonfuls so they do not soak into the bread too early.
Arrange apple slices, pickled onions, and salad leaves around the cheese to give fresh sharp contrast.
Add ham if using, folding it loosely so the plate still looks like a simple pub-style lunch rather than a sandwich.
Season the cheese and salad lightly with black pepper, avoiding too much salt because the cheese and pickles are savoury.
Let the board sit at room temperature for a few minutes so the cheese tastes fuller and less fridge-cold.
Serve as a no-cook lunch with extra bread or crackers, encouraging each bite to combine cheese, pickle, and crunch.

title: Bread Pudding
description: A dense old-fashioned British bread pudding packed with dried fruit, spice, and a crisp sugar top.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
instructions: Tear the stale bread into a large bowl, pour over the milk, and leave it to soak until completely soft.
Mash the soaked bread with clean hands or a spoon until no dry chunks remain and the mixture looks thick.
Stir in dried fruit, brown sugar, melted butter, beaten egg, mixed spice, vanilla, and a small pinch of salt.
Spread the mixture into a greased baking dish, pressing it into the corners so the pudding bakes evenly.
Sprinkle demerara sugar over the top to create the traditional crunchy sweet crust as it bakes.
Bake until the pudding is firm, deeply browned, and pulling slightly from the sides of the dish.
Cool for at least fifteen minutes before slicing, because the pudding sets as it rests and cuts more neatly.
Serve warm or cold, plain or with custard, keeping the texture dense, fruity, and gently spiced.

title: Sticky Toffee Pudding
description: A soft date sponge drenched in warm toffee sauce for a beloved British pub dessert.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
ingredients: 100 g dark brown sugar, for sauce
instructions: Soak the chopped dates in boiling water with baking soda until soft, then mash lightly so they blend into the sponge.
Cream butter and brown sugar until fluffy, then beat in the eggs one at a time with a little flour if needed.
Fold in flour, baking powder, vanilla, and the warm date mixture until the batter is smooth but not overmixed.
Spoon the batter into a buttered baking dish or individual moulds, levelling the tops for even rising.
Bake until the sponge springs back lightly and a skewer comes out with only moist crumbs attached.
Simmer cream, dark brown sugar, and butter together until glossy, thickened, and clearly toffee-scented.
Prick the hot sponge and pour over some sauce so it soaks in before the pudding reaches the table.
Serve warm with extra toffee sauce and cream or ice cream, keeping the sponge moist and the sauce generous.
